subject: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses

messages.author: 2725bf9dffb6e75f
messages.subject: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses
parts:
Hello,

I am running both PGLS (procD.pgls) and PPLS (phylo.integration) analyses to test for the significance of ecology as a predictor of skull shape in snakes. For procD.pgls, categorical ecological variables were used as the independent variables (i.e. all species with landmark data were categorically coded as arboreal, terrestrial etc., diurnal, nocturnal, etc., diet as amphibians, reptiles, etc.). For the PPLS analysis, quantitative diet data, (a matrix of proportions of each type of prey consumed), was used for the second block. Separate analyses were run for each of 8 snake skull elements (i.e. 8 different landmark subsets), and the ecological variables were found to be significant predictors of shape in all but a couple of cases (across all landmark subsets and ecological variables). 

This seemed like a red flag to me, so I proceeded to randomly permute my ecological data, creating 1000 random ecological datasets. I then re-ran the analyses and found that I am getting significant results far more often than I should be with the randomly permuted datasets (between 40-70% of the time depending on the landmark subset and ecological variable in question, α=0.05, n=1000) for both PGLS and PPLS analyses. I am not sure what could possibly be driving this or if there is simply something I am missing in the usage of these functions. 

I would really appreciate any thoughts or explanations as to what may be going on here.

Thanks,
Greg

Here is an example portion of the script I used to run the analyses:

# Landmarks aligned prior to this

# Loading categorical data for habitat use, temporal activity, and major diet category from csv file (for PGLS analysis)

Ecological_Data<-read.csv("Ecological_Data.csv", row.names=1)


# Loading quantitative data for diet proportions (for PPLS analysis)

Quantitative_Diet<-read.csv("Diet_Quantitative_Proportions.csv", row.names=1)


# Tree for PGLS

Zaher_tree<-read.tree("Zaher_2019_Phylogeny_SpeciesLandmarked")


# Tree for PPLS

Zaher_tree_PPLS<-keep.tip(Zaher_tree, diet_labels)


# Creating data frame for subsequent PGLS analyses

Zaher_notroph<-geomorph.data.frame(coords=aligned_notroph_phylo, Habitat_Use=Ecological_Data[,1], Activity=Ecological_Data[,2], Diet=Ecological_Data[,3], phy=Zaher_tree)


# PPLS Analysis for Non-Trophic Landmark Subset

phylo.integration(A=aligned_notroph_diet, A2=Quantitative_Diet, Zaher_tree_PPLS)


# PGLS Analysis for Non-Trophic Landmark Subset

summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Habitat_Use+Activity+Diet, phy=phy, data=Zaher_notroph, SS.type="III"))

messages.subject: Re: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses
parts:
Hello,

To append some additional information to my original question, I should also mention that r-squared valued when running the PGLS test have been behaving strangely. With my original dataset of ~110 species, procD.pgls was returning very homogenous r-squared values in the ballpark of 0.1-0.15 for every independent variable across all 8 skull elements (landmark subsets) separately analyzed. After increasing my dataset to its current size of 160 species, procD.pgls returned r-squared values that were either very high (~0.8) or very low (~0.02), with no intermediate values, across all three independent variables and across all landmark subsets.

I recently ran another randomization test with the goal of determining what the r-squared values would look like with randomized ecological data (done in the same way as when I did this for significance values above). I've attached some rough plots of what the r-squared values are looking like with randomized ecological data (for each of the three independent variables) over the course of 100 iterations of the randomization test. Strangely, the values seem to gravitate towards either ~0.8 or ~0.02, the same values I was seeing with my original, non-randomized data. 

I have talked to a couple of people in my lab about this, as well as my advisor, and they were baffled as to what the issue could be. I would really appreciate any thoughts folks might have.

Thanks,
Greg

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Re: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses
parts:
Greg,

 

It is impossible to know what is going on with your particular dataset from the descriptions so far. One comment I will make however is that your randomization approach is not a formal test of the method itself, nor does it necessarily reveal a pathology. For this, one must generate actual random data under a null model with a known pattern (read: permuting data will still have the peculiarities of those data in them: they are not necessarily examples of ‘null random’ pattern!). Thus, such evaluations are more apt to reveal curiosities of a particular data set and/or phylogeny rather than the method itself.

 

Without knowing more on what your data have and what you have done with them, I can only remind folks that the behavior for any particular dataset also depends on how the categorical variable is distributed on the phylogeny. We investigated this for phylogenetic anova last year and found that the extent to which the factor levels of the categorical variable ‘associate’ with phylogenetic clusters of taxa (ie subclades) can have a substantial effect on downstream phylogenetic anova (see Adams and Collyer 2018: Evolution).  This is not a problem with phylogenetic anova per se, but rather an unappreciated fact of the extent to which the categorical variable displays phylogenetic signal. We propose a means of investigating this in the paper via PLS.

 

For your particular example, it is impossible to know whether this is resulting in outcomes that you do not expect (though where the expectations come from is also something to consider). Regardless, I suggest you investigate this a bit more as per above to see the extent to which this provides insight.

 

I hope I’ve understood your question(s) sufficiently to point you in a good direction. If not, please let me know off-line and I can try to find time to discuss some more.


Best,

 

Dean
